name: Jesus Christ
summary: Jesus of Nazareth, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem in the days of Herod the Great, grew up in Nazareth as the son (as was supposed) of Joseph the carpenter. After his baptism by John in the Jordan he proclaimed the Kingdom of God in Galilee and Judea, called the Twelve, healed the sick, forgave sins, raised the dead and revealed the Father. At the Last Supper he instituted the Eucharist; he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, died and was buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, promising and sending the Holy Spirit upon his Church.
catholic: The Church confesses Jesus Christ as one divine Person in two natures, true God and true man: 'consubstantial with the Father' (Nicaea, 325) and consubstantial with us, his natures united without confusion, change, division or separation (Chalcedon, 451; CCC 464-469). In the Incarnation the eternal Word took flesh of the Virgin Mary by the power of the Holy Spirit (Jn 1:14; CCC 461-463). His Passion, death, Resurrection and Ascension - the Paschal Mystery - accomplish our redemption and are made present in the liturgy, above all in the Eucharist he instituted at the Last Supper, 'the source and summit of the Christian life' (CCC 1324). He founded his Church on the apostles, with Peter as the rock (Mt 16:18), and remains present to it in word and sacrament until he comes again. Scripture presents him as the New Adam, the Son of David and heir of the promises to Abraham, the new Moses, one greater than Jonah and Solomon, and the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets (Mt 5:17; Lk 24:27).
know: True God and true man: one divine Person in two natures (Council of Chalcedon, 451).

feast: December 25 (Christmas); Easter Sunday (movable); also the Epiphany, the Presentation (February 2), the Transfiguration (August 6), Corpus Christi, the Sacred Heart and Christ the King

name: Mary, Mother of Jesus
summary: A virgin of Nazareth betrothed to Joseph, Mary was greeted by the angel Gabriel and conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit, answering 'let it be done to me according to your word'. She visited her relative Elizabeth and sang the Magnificat, gave birth in Bethlehem, presented Jesus in the Temple and found him there at twelve. She prompted his first sign at Cana, stood by the cross where Jesus entrusted her to the beloved disciple, and prayed with the apostles awaiting the Spirit.
catholic: The Church professes four Marian dogmas: Mary is the Mother of God (Theotokos), defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 (CCC 495); she is ever-virgin, before, during and after the birth of Christ (CCC 496-507); she was preserved from all stain of original sin from her conception (Immaculate Conception, defined by Pius IX in 1854; CCC 490-492); and she was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory (Assumption, defined by Pius XII in 1950; CCC 966). The Fathers call her the New Eve, whose obedience untied the knot of Eve's disobedience (St Irenaeus, CCC 494), and she is the Ark of the Covenant where the glory of the Lord dwells (CCC 2676) - Luke's Visitation deliberately echoes David bringing up the Ark (2 Sam 6). From the cross Jesus gave her as mother to the beloved disciple (Jn 19:26-27), which the Church reads as her spiritual motherhood of all believers (CCC 964-970). The 'brothers' of Jesus are understood as kinsmen, not further children of Mary (CCC 500).

Tradition (Protoevangelium of James), not Scripture, names her parents Joachim and Anne.

name: Joseph, husband of Mary
summary: A righteous man of the house of David, Joseph was betrothed to Mary. When she was found with child by the Holy Spirit, an angel told him in a dream to take her as his wife and to name the child Jesus. He brought the family to Bethlehem for the census, fled with them into Egypt from Herod, and settled in Nazareth, where Jesus was known as 'the carpenter's son'.
catholic: St Joseph is honoured as the chaste spouse of the Virgin Mary and the legal and foster father of Jesus, through whom Jesus is legally 'son of David' (Mt 1:16, 20); the Church teaches he was not Jesus' natural father (CCC 496-497). Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870, and Pope Francis opened a Year of St Joseph (2020-2021) with the letter Patris Corde. Because tradition holds that he died with Jesus and Mary beside him, he is invoked as patron of a happy death (CCC 1014), as well as of workers and families. Like Joseph son of Jacob, he is a dreamer who goes down to Egypt to save his family.

name: Joachim
summary: Scripture does not name the Virgin Mary's parents. Tradition, beginning with the second-century Protoevangelium of James, names her father Joachim, a devout and prosperous man who with his wife Anne prayed long for a child.
catholic: Tradition holds that Joachim and Anne received Mary as the answer to their prayers and presented her in the Temple (commemorated on November 21). The Church honours them together as the grandparents of Jesus, and Pope Francis instituted (2021) the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly on the fourth Sunday of July, close to their feast. Their story is not Scripture, but the liturgy honours them as the parents through whom God prepared the Immaculate Mother of his Son.

name: Anne

catholic: Tradition holds that Anne conceived Mary after years of barrenness and prayer, and the Church celebrates Mary's Immaculate Conception in Anne's womb (December 8) and her Nativity (September 8). name: Elizabeth
summary: Elizabeth, of the priestly line of Aaron and wife of the priest Zechariah, was righteous but barren and advanced in years. She conceived John in her old age, and when her relative Mary visited, the child leapt in her womb and, filled with the Holy Spirit, she greeted Mary as 'the mother of my Lord'. At John's circumcision she insisted he be named John.
catholic: Elizabeth's inspired words 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb' form part of the Hail Mary (CCC 2676), and her greeting of Mary as 'the mother of my Lord' is cited by the Church for Mary's divine motherhood (CCC 495). The Visitation (May 31) celebrates her meeting with Mary. Her late, miraculous motherhood echoes Sarah and Hannah and shows that 'nothing is impossible with God' (Lk 1:37).

name: Zechariah (Zacharias)
role: Priest; father of John the Baptist
summary: Zechariah was a priest of the division of Abijah. While he offered incense in the Temple, the angel Gabriel announced that his barren wife Elizabeth would bear a son to be named John; because he doubted, he was struck mute. When he wrote 'His name is John', his speech returned and he prophesied the Benedictus.
catholic: Zechariah's canticle, the Benedictus (Lk 1:68-79), is prayed every day at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, blessing God for the dawn of salvation and for John's mission as prophet of the Most High. His muteness and restored speech are often contrasted with Mary's faith-filled question at the Annunciation. He and Elizabeth are commemorated together as saints.

name: John the Baptist
summary: Son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, John lived in the wilderness, wore camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He preached a baptism of repentance in the Jordan, baptized Jesus, and pointed him out as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world'. Imprisoned by Herod Antipas for condemning his marriage to Herodias, he was beheaded at the request of Herodias's daughter.
catholic: John is the Lord's immediate precursor, 'more than a prophet', the last of the prophets of the Old Covenant and the voice foretold by Isaiah (CCC 523, 717-720). Jesus identifies him with the Elijah who was to come (Mt 11:14). His words 'Behold the Lamb of God' are repeated at every Mass before Communion. Besides Christ and Mary he is the only saint whose birth is celebrated in the calendar (June 24), and his martyrdom is kept on August 29. He is honoured as a martyr for truth and for the sanctity of marriage.

name: James, 'brother of the Lord'
role: Kinsman of Jesus; leader of the Jerusalem Church
summary: Named first among Jesus' 'brothers' at Nazareth (Mt 13:55; Mk 6:3), James is 'James the less' whose mother Mary watched at the cross (Mk 15:40). The risen Christ appeared to him (1 Cor 15:7), and he became a leader of the church in Jerusalem, speaking decisively at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:13-21). Paul calls him 'the Lord's brother' and one of the pillars of the Church (Gal 1:19; 2:9).
catholic: Following St Jerome, the Church understands 'brother' here in the broad biblical sense of kinsman: James and Joses are sons of another Mary, not of the Virgin Mary (CCC 500). Catholic tradition generally identifies him with the apostle James son of Alphaeus ('St James the Less') and as author of the Letter of James, whose instruction on anointing the sick is the scriptural basis of that sacrament (Jas 5:14-15; CCC 1510). Tradition (Hegesippus) and the historian Josephus record his death by stoning in Jerusalem around AD 62.

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:28).
Son of Er; father of Cosam.

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:28).

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:29).

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:30).
Son of Judah; father of Levi.

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:30).
Son of Joseph; father of Simeon.

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:30).
Son of Jonan; father of Judah.

know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:30).
Son of Eliakim; father of Joseph.

name: Eliakim
summary: Eliakim, son of Melea, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Jonan (Lk 3:30).
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:30).
Son of Melea; father of Jonan.

name: Melea
summary: Melea, son of Menan, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Eliakim (Lk 3:31).
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:31).
Son of Menan; father of Eliakim.

name: Menan
summary: Menan, son of Mattatha, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Melea (Lk 3:31).
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:31).
Son of Mattatha; father of Melea.

name: Mattatha
summary: Mattatha, son of Nathan son of David, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Menan (Lk 3:31).
catholic: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back to Adam, 'the son of God' (Lk 3:38), showing him as Saviour of the whole human race; unlike Matthew, his line descends through David's son Nathan rather than Solomon.
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:31).
Son of Nathan son of David; father of Menan.

name: Cainan, son of Arphaxad
summary: Cainan appears in Luke's genealogy between Arphaxad and Shelah ('the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad', Lk 3:35-36). He is absent from the Hebrew text of Genesis 11 but present in the Greek Septuagint, which Luke follows.
know: Named only in Luke 3:36 (and the Septuagint of Genesis 11).
Distinct from Cainan (Kenan) son of Enos in Luke 3:37.
Shows Luke's use of the Greek Old Testament.

name: Peter
summary: Simon, a Galilean fisherman from Bethsaida living at Capernaum, was brought to Jesus by his brother Andrew and renamed Cephas, 'Rock' (Peter). He confessed Jesus as 'the Christ, the Son of the living God', received the keys of the Kingdom, witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane, and denied Jesus three times during the Passion. The risen Lord appeared to him and three times charged him to feed his sheep; in Acts he leads the Church, preaching at Pentecost and receiving the first Gentiles.
catholic: Jesus' words 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church ... I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven' (Mt 16:18-19) ground the Petrine office: Peter is to strengthen his brethren (Lk 22:32) and feed Christ's flock (Jn 21:15-17), a ministry continued by his successors, the Bishops of Rome (CCC 552-553, 881). The Church is built on the faith he confessed (CCC 424). Tradition holds he was crucified head downward in Rome under Nero, and St Peter's Basilica stands over his tomb. His triple denial and triple profession of love make him a model of repentance and mercy.
know: Son of John/Jonah and brother of Andrew (Jn 1:40-42; Mt 16:17).
Married: Jesus healed his mother-in-law (Mk 1:29-31).
Always named first in the lists of the Twelve (Mt 10:2).
Traditionally the author of 1 and 2 Peter; Mark's Gospel is said to preserve his preaching.
Feasts June 29 (Sts Peter and Paul) and February 22 (Chair of St Peter).
feast: June 29 (Sts Peter and Paul); February 22 (Chair of St Peter)

relations.type: apostle of; confessed him the Christ
spoke with at the Council of Jerusalem

name: Andrew
summary: A fisherman of Bethsaida and first a disciple of John the Baptist, Andrew followed Jesus when John called him the Lamb of God, and at once brought his brother Simon to Jesus. He pointed out the boy with five loaves and two fish at the feeding of the five thousand, and with Philip brought the Greeks who wished to see Jesus.
catholic: The Eastern Church calls him Protokletos, 'the First-Called' (Jn 1:40). Tradition holds he preached around the Black Sea and Greece and was crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross, the 'St Andrew's cross'. He is patron of Scotland, Russia and Greece, and of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, so his feast is a sign of Catholic-Orthodox friendship.
know: Brother of Simon Peter; son of John/Jonah.
First a disciple of John the Baptist (Jn 1:35-40).
Brought Peter to Jesus (Jn 1:41-42).
Feast November 30.

relations.type: brother of; brought him to Jesus

name: John (Jonah), father of Peter
summary: The father of Simon Peter and Andrew is named in Jesus' words 'Simon Bar Jonah' (Mt 16:17) and 'Simon son of Jonah' (Jn 1:42; 21:15-17).
know: The World English Bible reads 'Jonah'; many manuscripts and translations of John read 'John'.
Father of the apostles Peter and Andrew.

name: Peter's mother-in-law
summary: Simon Peter's mother-in-law lay sick with a fever in the house at Capernaum; Jesus took her by the hand, the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
catholic: Her immediate service after healing is read as a model of the grace that frees us for service. The episode also shows that Peter was married.
know: Unnamed in Scripture.
Healed in Peter's house at Capernaum (Mk 1:29-31).
Shows that Peter was married.

name: James, son of Zebedee
summary: James and his brother John were fishermen, partners of Simon, who left their father Zebedee in the boat to follow Jesus. Named 'Boanerges', Sons of Thunder, he belonged with Peter and John to the inner circle present at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. He was the first of the Twelve to be martyred, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa I.
catholic: Known as St James the Greater to distinguish him from James the Less. His request for a place of glory led Jesus to teach that he would drink his cup, fulfilled in his martyrdom (Mk 10:38-39; Acts 12:2). Tradition holds his relics rest at Santiago de Compostela, goal of the great pilgrimage, and he is patron of Spain and of pilgrims.
know: Son of Zebedee; brother of John (Mt 4:21).
With Peter and John, witness of the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1).
First apostle martyred (Acts 12:2).
Feast July 25.

name: John, son of Zebedee
summary: John, a fisherman and brother of James, left his father Zebedee to follow Jesus and with Peter and James formed the inner circle of the Twelve. He and Peter prepared the Passover and later preached together in Jerusalem and Samaria. Catholic tradition identifies him with 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', who leaned on Jesus' breast at the Last Supper, stood at the cross and received Mary as his mother, and ran to the empty tomb.
catholic: The Church honours John as Apostle and Evangelist, by tradition author of the Fourth Gospel, three letters and the Book of Revelation, whose symbol is the eagle. In receiving Mary at the foot of the cross (Jn 19:26-27) he represents every disciple entrusted to her motherly care (CCC 964). Paul names him a 'pillar' of the Church (Gal 2:9). Tradition holds he was exiled to Patmos and died in old age at Ephesus, the only apostle not martyred.
know: Son of Zebedee; brother of James; called Boanerges (Mk 3:17).
Traditionally 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (Jn 13:23; 19:26).
Took Mary into his home (Jn 19:27).
Traditionally the author of John, 1-3 John and Revelation.
Feast December 27.

name: Zebedee
role: Fisherman; father of James and John
summary: Zebedee was a Galilean fisherman with hired servants, mending nets in the boat with his sons James and John when Jesus called them; they left him and followed Jesus.
know: Father of the apostles James and John (Mt 4:21).
Ran a fishing business with hired men (Mk 1:20).
His wife is generally identified with Salome (compare Mt 27:56 with Mk 15:40).

name: Salome
aliases: mother of the sons of Zebedee
role: Disciple; mother of James and John
summary: Salome was among the women who followed Jesus from Galilee, watched the crucifixion, and came with spices to anoint his body on Easter morning (Mk 15:40; 16:1). Comparing Mark with Matthew's 'mother of the sons of Zebedee' (Mt 27:56), she is generally identified as the mother of James and John, who asked Jesus that her sons sit at his right and left in his Kingdom.
catholic: Her request prompted Jesus' teaching that greatness in the Kingdom means service and drinking his cup (Mt 20:20-28). Some interpreters also identify her with the sister of Jesus' mother at the cross (Jn 19:25), which would make James and John kinsmen of Jesus; this is uncertain. She is honoured among the myrrh-bearing women, first witnesses of the empty tomb.
know: Named only in Mark (Mk 15:40; 16:1).
Generally identified with 'the mother of the sons of Zebedee' (Mt 20:20; 27:56).
Brought spices to the tomb on Easter morning.

relations.type: asked places of honour for her sons from

names: mother of the sons of Zebedee

name: Philip
summary: Philip of Bethsaida was called by Jesus with the words 'Follow me' and at once brought Nathanael, saying 'Come and see'. Jesus tested him before feeding the five thousand; Greeks seeking Jesus came to him; and at the Last Supper he asked, 'Lord, show us the Father'.
catholic: Jesus' reply to Philip, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (Jn 14:9), is a key text for the unity of the Son with the Father. Tradition holds he preached in Asia Minor and was martyred at Hierapolis. He shares a feast with St James the Less, whose relics with his rest in the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles in Rome. He is distinct from Philip the deacon and evangelist of Acts.
know: From Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (Jn 1:44).
Brought Nathanael to Jesus (Jn 1:45-46).
'Lord, show us the Father' (Jn 14:8).
Feast May 3, with St James the Less.

name: Bartholomew (Nathanael)
summary: Bartholomew appears in every list of the Twelve, usually beside Philip. Catholic tradition identifies him with Nathanael of Cana, whom Philip brought to Jesus: Jesus called him 'an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit', and he confessed, 'Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!'
catholic: The name Bartholomew is a patronymic ('son of Tolmai'), which is why he can also bear the personal name Nathanael; the identification is traditional rather than certain. Jesus' promise to him of 'angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (Jn 1:51) presents Christ as Jacob's ladder. Tradition holds he preached in India and Armenia and was flayed alive.
know: Paired with Philip in the lists of the Twelve (Mt 10:3).
Traditionally identified with Nathanael of Cana (Jn 1:45-51; 21:2).
Confessed Jesus as Son of God and King of Israel (Jn 1:49).
Feast August 24.

name: Matthew (Levi)
summary: Matthew, also called Levi son of Alphaeus, was a tax collector at Capernaum. At Jesus' word 'Follow me' he left his tax booth and hosted a banquet for Jesus with tax collectors and sinners, where Jesus said he came to call not the righteous but sinners.
catholic: The Church honours him as Apostle and Evangelist, by tradition author of the First Gospel, written to show Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's Scriptures; his symbol is the man (or angel). His call, painted by Caravaggio, is a classic image of grace meeting a sinner. Tradition holds he died a martyr.
know: Called 'Levi the son of Alphaeus' in Mark 2:14.
A tax collector (Mt 9:9; 10:3).
Traditionally author of the Gospel of Matthew.
Feast September 21.

relations.type: called from the tax office by

name: Alphaeus, father of Levi
summary: Alphaeus is named once, as the father of Levi the tax collector (Mk 2:14), whom the other Gospels call Matthew.
know: Named only in Mark 2:14.
Whether he is the same Alphaeus as the father of James is not stated in Scripture.

name: Thomas (Didymus)
summary: Thomas, called Didymus ('Twin'), urged the disciples to go with Jesus to Judea 'that we may die with him', and asked at the Last Supper how they could know the way. Absent when the risen Jesus first appeared, he refused to believe without touching the wounds; a week later Jesus invited him to do so, and he confessed, 'My Lord and my God!'
catholic: Thomas's confession is one of the clearest New Testament professions of Christ's divinity (CCC 448), and Jesus' reply - 'Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed' - is addressed to every later believer. Tradition holds he evangelized India, where the 'St Thomas Christians' trace their origin to him, and was martyred near Chennai.
know: Called Didymus, 'the Twin' (Jn 11:16).
Asked 'How can we know the way?' - 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (Jn 14:5-6).
Confessed 'My Lord and my God!' (Jn 20:28).
Feast July 3.

name: James, son of Alphaeus
summary: James son of Alphaeus is the ninth name in the lists of the Twelve (Mt 10:3; Mk 3:18; Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13); nothing else is said of him under that name.
catholic: Catholic tradition generally identifies him with 'James the less' (Mk 15:40) and with James 'the brother of the Lord' who led the Jerusalem church, and honours him as St James the Less together with St Philip. The identification is traditional rather than certain.
know: Son of Alphaeus (Mt 10:3).
Traditionally 'St James the Less'.
Catholic tradition generally identifies him with James the brother of the Lord.
Feast May 3, with St Philip.

name: Alphaeus
summary: Alphaeus is known only as the father of the apostle James (Mt 10:3; Mk 3:18; Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13).
know: Father of James son of Alphaeus.
Some ancient writers identified him with Clopas (Jn 19:25); this is uncertain.
Scripture does not say whether he is the same as Levi's father (Mk 2:14).

name: Jude Thaddeus
summary: The apostle is called 'Judas the son of James' in Luke and Acts and 'Thaddaeus' (Matthew also 'Lebbaeus') in Matthew and Mark. At the Last Supper 'Judas (not Iscariot)' asked why Jesus would reveal himself to the disciples and not to the world, and Jesus answered that he and the Father would make their home with whoever loves him.
catholic: Catholic tradition often identifies him with Jude, 'brother of James', author of the Letter of Jude, reading Luke's Greek 'Judas of James' as 'brother of James' (as the Douay-Rheims does). Tradition holds he preached with Simon the Zealot in Persia, where both were martyred, so they share a feast. He is widely invoked as patron of desperate and lost causes.
know: Called Thaddaeus (Mk 3:18) and 'Judas the son of James' (Lk 6:16).
'Judas (not Iscariot)' of John 14:22.
Patron of hopeless causes.
Feast October 28, with St Simon.

name: Simon the Zealot
summary: Simon, called 'the Zealot', appears in each list of the Twelve (Mt 10:4; Mk 3:18; Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13), distinguished from Simon Peter by his surname.
catholic: His surname may point to zeal for the Law or to the nationalist movement; either way, Jesus gathered into one band a former 'zealot' and a former tax collector (Matthew). Tradition holds he preached with Jude in Persia, where both were martyred, so they share a feast.
know: Called 'the Zealot' to distinguish him from Peter.
Nothing else is recorded of him in Scripture.
Feast October 28, with St Jude.

name: Judas Iscariot
summary: Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, was one of the Twelve and kept the common purse, from which he stole. He agreed with the chief priests to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, left the Last Supper into the night, and handed Jesus over in Gethsemane with a kiss. Seized with remorse, he returned the silver and hanged himself; Matthias was chosen to take his place.
catholic: Judas shows that even one chosen and close to Christ can freely refuse grace. The Fathers contrast him with Peter: both failed, but Peter repented and trusted in mercy while Judas despaired. Matthew sees the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field as fulfilment of prophecy (Mt 27:9-10). The Church does not declare any individual damned, but Jesus' own words about him are grave (Mt 26:24).
know: Son of Simon Iscariot (Jn 6:71).
Betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Mt 26:14-16).
Betrayed him with a kiss (Lk 22:47-48).
Replaced among the Twelve by Matthias (Acts 1:26).

name: Simon Iscariot
summary: Simon Iscariot is named only as the father of Judas the betrayer (Jn 6:71; 13:26).
know: Father of Judas Iscariot.
Named only in John's Gospel.

name: Mary Magdalene
summary: Mary of Magdala, from whom Jesus cast out seven demons, followed him from Galilee and supported him from her means. She stood by the cross, saw where he was buried, and came to the tomb early on Easter morning. The risen Jesus appeared first to her, calling her by name, and sent her to tell the disciples, 'I have seen the Lord'.
catholic: Because she was sent to announce the Resurrection to the apostles, Christian tradition - St Hippolytus called the myrrh-bearing women 'apostles to the apostles', and St Thomas Aquinas uses the title - honours her as 'Apostle of the Apostles', and in 2016 Pope Francis raised her memorial to a feast. She is honoured among the holy women who were the first witnesses of the Resurrection (CCC 641). Western tradition since St Gregory the Great identified her with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary of Bethany; the reformed Roman calendar (1969) treats them as distinct.
know: Seven demons were cast out of her (Lk 8:2; Mk 16:9).
Present at the crucifixion, the burial and the empty tomb.
First to see the risen Lord (Jn 20:11-18; Mk 16:9).
Feast July 22.

relations.type: brought news of the empty tomb to

name: Martha
summary: Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, welcomed Jesus into her home and was 'distracted with much serving' while Mary listened at his feet. When Lazarus died she went out to meet Jesus and professed, 'I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God'; at the supper in Bethany before the Passion she again served.
catholic: Martha's confession of faith at Lazarus's tomb (Jn 11:27) parallels Peter's, and Jesus' words to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life', are read at funerals. With Mary she is classically read as the active life beside the contemplative. In 2021 Pope Francis extended her memorial on July 29 to include her sister Mary and brother Lazarus. She is patron of cooks, servers and hospitality.
know: Sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany (Jn 11:1).
'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things' (Lk 10:41).
Confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God (Jn 11:27).
Feast July 29 (Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus).

relations.type: confessed the Christ, the Son of God

name: Mary of Bethany
summary: Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, sat at Jesus' feet listening to his word, and Jesus said she had 'chosen the good part'. When Lazarus died she fell at Jesus' feet weeping. Six days before the Passover she anointed Jesus' feet with costly nard and wiped them with her hair, an act Jesus linked to his burial.
catholic: Mary is the model of contemplative listening to the Word. John identifies her with the woman who anointed Jesus at Bethany (Jn 11:2; 12:3; compare Mt 26:6-13; Mk 14:3-9), of whom Jesus said that what she did would be told wherever the Gospel is preached. Western tradition long identified her with Mary Magdalene; since 2021 she is celebrated with Martha and Lazarus on July 29.
know: Sister of Martha and Lazarus (Jn 11:1).
'Mary has chosen the good part' (Lk 10:42).
Anointed Jesus' feet with nard (Jn 12:3).
Feast July 29 (Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus).

name: Lazarus of Bethany
role: Friend of Jesus, raised from the dead
summary: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, was a friend whom Jesus loved. When he fell ill and died, Jesus came after four days, wept, and called him from the tomb: 'Lazarus, come out!' Many believed, and the chief priests plotted to kill both Jesus and Lazarus.
catholic: The raising of Lazarus, the greatest of Jesus' signs in John, reveals him as 'the resurrection and the life' and anticipates his own Resurrection, though Lazarus returned to an ordinary, mortal life (CCC 646). It is the Gospel of the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year A, used for the third scrutiny of those preparing for Baptism. Eastern tradition holds he later became bishop of Kition in Cyprus. Since 2021 he is honoured with his sisters on July 29.
know: Brother of Martha and Mary (Jn 11:1-2).
'Jesus wept' at his tomb (Jn 11:35).
Raised after four days in the tomb (Jn 11:39-44).
Feast July 29 (Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus).

name: Lazarus (the beggar in the parable)
summary: In Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus, a poor man covered with sores lay at a rich man's gate; at death he was carried by angels to Abraham's bosom while the rich man suffered torment. Abraham told the rich man that those who will not hear Moses and the prophets would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead.
catholic: Lazarus is the only named character in any of Jesus' parables. The Church cites the parable for the 'bosom of Abraham' where the just awaited Christ (CCC 633), for the immediate judgment after death, and as a summons to recognize Christ in the poor (CCC 2463).
know: The only named character in a parable of Jesus.
Carried to 'Abraham's bosom' (Lk 16:22).
Distinct from Lazarus of Bethany.

name: Joanna
summary: Joanna, wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas, was healed by Jesus and with other women supported him and the Twelve from her means. She was among the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles.
catholic: Joanna shows the Gospel reaching even Herod's court. She is honoured among the myrrh-bearing women, the first heralds of the Resurrection.
know: Wife of Chuza, Herod's steward (Lk 8:3).
Provided for Jesus and the Twelve from her possessions.
Witness of the empty tomb (Lk 24:10).

name: Chuza
summary: Chuza (Chuzas) was the steward of Herod Antipas and husband of Joanna, one of the women who followed and supported Jesus.
know: Husband of Joanna (Lk 8:3).
A household official of Herod Antipas.

name: Susanna (follower of Jesus)
summary: Susanna is named among the women who had been healed by Jesus and who travelled with him and the Twelve, providing for them from their possessions (Lk 8:3).
know: Named once, in Luke 8:3.
Distinct from Susanna of the Book of Daniel.

name: Nicodemus
role: Pharisee; ruler of the Jews; disciple
summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin, came to Jesus by night and was taught that one must be born of water and the Spirit to enter the Kingdom of God. Later he urged the council to give Jesus a fair hearing, and after the crucifixion he brought about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes to help Joseph of Arimathea bury Jesus.
catholic: Jesus' words to Nicodemus, 'unless one is born of water and the Spirit' (Jn 3:5), are a foundational text for the necessity of Baptism (CCC 1215, 1257), and the same discourse contains 'God so loved the world' (Jn 3:16). He is cited with Joseph of Arimathea as one of the religious leaders who were secret disciples (CCC 595). His journey from night to open devotion models gradual conversion.
know: Came to Jesus by night (Jn 3:2).
Heard 'born of water and the Spirit' and 'God so loved the world' (Jn 3:5, 16).
Defended Jesus before the Pharisees (Jn 7:50-51).
Helped bury Jesus with myrrh and aloes (Jn 19:39).
feast: August 31 (Sts Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, Roman Martyrology)

name: Joseph of Arimathea
summary: Joseph of Arimathea was a rich and respected member of the council, a good and righteous man looking for the Kingdom of God, who had not consented to the council's decision. A secret disciple, he boldly asked Pilate for Jesus' body, wrapped it in clean linen and laid it in his own new tomb cut in the rock.
catholic: Joseph fulfils the prophecy that the Servant would be 'with a rich man in his death' (Is 53:9) and is cited with Nicodemus as a secret disciple among the leaders (CCC 595). His care for Jesus' body is honoured in the Fourteenth Station of the Cross and in the corporal work of mercy of burying the dead. Medieval legends link him with Glastonbury and the Holy Grail, but these are not historical tradition.
know: A rich council member from Arimathaea (Mt 27:57; Lk 23:50-51).
Asked Pilate for Jesus' body (Mk 15:43).
Laid Jesus in his own new tomb (Mt 27:60).
Commemorated with Nicodemus on August 31.
feast: August 31 (Sts Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, Roman Martyrology)

name: Zacchaeus
summary: Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector of Jericho, was short and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus. Jesus called him down and stayed at his house; Zacchaeus promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution to any he had defrauded, and Jesus declared, 'Today, salvation has come to this house'.
catholic: Zacchaeus is the Church's model of conversion shown in restitution: the Catechism cites his pledge in teaching that justice requires restoring what was unjustly taken (CCC 2412). His story is the Gospel for the Dedication of a Church, as Christ comes to dwell in his house, and ends with the mission statement 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost'.
know: Chief tax collector at Jericho (Lk 19:2).
Climbed a sycamore to see Jesus (Lk 19:4).
Promised fourfold restitution (Lk 19:8).
'Today, salvation has come to this house' (Lk 19:9).

name: Bartimaeus
summary: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, was a blind beggar at Jericho. Hearing that Jesus was passing, he cried out, 'Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!' and would not be silenced; throwing off his cloak he came to Jesus, received his sight, and followed him on the way.
catholic: His persistent cry joins the Gospel prayers of mercy that shaped the 'Jesus Prayer' and the Kyrie eleison. He confesses Jesus by the messianic title 'Son of David', and his following 'on the way' to Jerusalem makes him a model disciple.
know: Son of Timaeus (Mk 10:46).
Called Jesus 'Son of David' (Mk 10:47).
Healed at Jericho and followed Jesus (Mk 10:52).

name: Timaeus
summary: Timaeus is named only as the father of the blind beggar Bartimaeus of Jericho (Mk 10:46).
know: Father of Bartimaeus.
Named only in Mark 10:46.

name: Jairus
summary: Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, begged Jesus to come to his dying twelve-year-old daughter. While Jesus was delayed healing a woman with a flow of blood, word came that the girl had died; Jesus said, 'Don't be afraid, only believe', took her by the hand - 'Talitha cumi' - and raised her.
catholic: The raising of Jairus's daughter is one of the Gospel signs restoring the dead to earthly life that point to Christ's own, greater Resurrection (CCC 646). Jesus took only Peter, James and John with the parents, a sign of the inner circle.
know: A ruler of the synagogue (Mk 5:22).
'Don't be afraid, only believe' (Mk 5:36).
His daughter, aged twelve, was raised from the dead (Mk 5:41-42).

name: Simeon
role: Righteous man who received the Christ child
summary: Simeon, a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem awaiting the consolation of Israel, had been told by the Holy Spirit he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. When Mary and Joseph presented Jesus in the Temple, he took the child in his arms, blessed God, and foretold that Jesus would be a sign spoken against and that a sword would pierce Mary's soul.
catholic: Simeon's canticle, the Nunc Dimittis ('Now, Lord, you let your servant go in peace', Lk 2:29-32), is prayed every night at Night Prayer (Compline). At the Presentation (February 2) he recognizes Jesus as 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles', which gives the feast its candle blessing (Candlemas). The Church sees in the Presentation Christ's first offering of himself (CCC 529), and his prophecy is the first of the Seven Sorrows of Mary.
know: Promised he would see the Christ before death (Lk 2:26).
Took the infant Jesus in his arms in the Temple (Lk 2:28).
Spoke the Nunc Dimittis (Lk 2:29-32).
Prophesied the sword that would pierce Mary's soul (Lk 2:35).

name: Anna
summary: Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, was a widow of great age who never left the Temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. Coming up at the Presentation, she gave thanks to God and spoke of the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.
catholic: With Simeon, Anna represents faithful Israel waiting for the Messiah and welcoming him at the Presentation (CCC 529). Her life of prayer and fasting in the Temple makes her a patroness of widows and of consecrated life.
know: Daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (Lk 2:36).
A widow who served God in the Temple night and day (Lk 2:37).
Spoke of Jesus to all awaiting Jerusalem's redemption (Lk 2:38).

name: Phanuel
summary: Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, is named only as the father of Anna the prophetess (Lk 2:36).
know: Father of Anna (Lk 2:36).
Of the tribe of Asher.

name: Simon the leper
summary: In the house of Simon the leper at Bethany, a woman poured costly ointment on Jesus' head; Jesus defended her, saying she had anointed his body beforehand for burial.
know: His house at Bethany was the scene of the anointing before the Passion (Mt 26:6; Mk 14:3).
John places the Bethany anointing at the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary (Jn 12:1-3).
Distinct in the text from Simon the Pharisee (Lk 7).

name: Simon the Pharisee
summary: Simon, a Pharisee, invited Jesus to dine. When a sinful woman wept at Jesus' feet, wiped them with her hair and anointed them, Simon doubted Jesus was a prophet; Jesus told the parable of the two debtors and declared, 'Her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much'.
catholic: The episode teaches the link between forgiveness and love and is a classic text for the sacrament of Penance and for contrition born of love. Western tradition after St Gregory the Great identified the sinful woman with Mary Magdalene, a view the Church no longer assumes.
know: A Pharisee who hosted Jesus (Lk 7:36, 40).
Heard the parable of the two debtors (Lk 7:41-43).
Distinct in the text from Simon the leper of Bethany.

name: Simon of Cyrene
summary: Simon, a man of Cyrene coming in from the country, was compelled by the soldiers to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha. Mark names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus, evidently known to Mark's readers.
catholic: Simon is remembered in the Fifth Station of the Cross. Luke's phrase that he carried the cross 'after Jesus' (Lk 23:26) makes him an image of every disciple who takes up the cross and follows Christ (Lk 9:23).
know: From Cyrene in North Africa (Mt 27:32).
Compelled to carry Jesus' cross (Mk 15:21).
Father of Alexander and Rufus (Mk 15:21).

name: Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene
summary: Alexander is named, with his brother Rufus, as a son of Simon of Cyrene (Mk 15:21), apparently because they were known to Mark's readers.
know: Son of Simon of Cyrene.
Brother of Rufus.

name: Rufus, son of Simon of Cyrene
summary: Rufus is named, with his brother Alexander, as a son of Simon of Cyrene (Mk 15:21).
know: Son of Simon of Cyrene; brother of Alexander.
Possibly the Rufus 'chosen in the Lord' greeted in Romans 16:13, since Mark is traditionally linked with Rome; this is uncertain.

name: Malchus
summary: Malchus was the servant of the high priest whose right ear Simon Peter cut off with a sword at Jesus' arrest. Jesus ordered Peter to put away the sword, and Luke records that he touched the ear and healed it.
catholic: The scene shows Christ freely accepting his Passion ('the cup which the Father has given me') and healing even an enemy, his last miracle before the cross.
know: Servant of the high priest (Jn 18:10).
His ear was cut off by Peter (Jn 18:10).
Healed by Jesus (Lk 22:51).

name: Barabbas
summary: Barabbas was a notorious prisoner, held for insurrection and murder, whom Pilate offered to release at the Passover alongside Jesus. Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd chose Barabbas and demanded that Jesus be crucified.
catholic: The Fathers noted that his name means 'son of the father': the guilty 'son of the father' goes free while the innocent Son of the Father dies in his place, an image of Christ's substitutionary sacrifice for sinners.
know: A 'notable prisoner' (Mt 27:16).
Imprisoned for insurrection and murder (Mk 15:7; Lk 23:19).
Released by Pilate at the crowd's demand (Mk 15:15).

name: Theophilus
summary: Theophilus is the 'most excellent' person to whom Luke dedicates his Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, so that he may know the certainty of what he has been taught.
catholic: His title suggests a person of rank, perhaps Luke's patron. Since the name means 'friend of God', the Fathers (e.g. St Ambrose) also read it as addressing every reader who loves God.
know: Addressee of Luke 1:3 and Acts 1:1.
Name means 'friend of God' or 'loved by God'.
Called 'most excellent', a title of rank.

name: Herod the Great
summary: Herod, an Idumean made king of Judea by Rome, ruled from 37 to 4 BC and rebuilt the Jerusalem Temple on a grand scale. Troubled by the Magi's news of a newborn King of the Jews, he ordered the killing of the boys of Bethlehem; Joseph fled with Jesus and Mary into Egypt until Herod died.
catholic: The Holy Innocents he massacred are honoured as martyrs on December 28, having died in place of Christ. His hostility to the newborn King recalls Pharaoh's slaughter of Hebrew infants and casts Jesus as the new Moses (Mt 2:15-18). The Temple he expanded is the one Jesus knew (Jn 2:20).
know: King of Judea when Jesus and John the Baptist were born (Mt 2:1; Lk 1:5).
Ordered the massacre of the Innocents (Mt 2:16).
Father of Archelaus, Antipas and Philip; grandfather of Herodias and Herod Agrippa I (Josephus).

name: Archelaus
summary: Archelaus, son of Herod the Great, ruled Judea, Samaria and Idumea after his father's death (4 BC - AD 6) until Rome deposed him for misrule. Fearing him, Joseph withdrew with the child and Mary to Galilee and settled in Nazareth.
catholic: Many commentators see an echo of his journey to Rome to receive his kingdom, and the delegation sent against him, in Jesus' parable of the nobleman (Lk 19:12-14).
know: Son of Herod the Great (Mt 2:22).
His reign is why the Holy Family settled in Nazareth (Mt 2:22-23).
Deposed by Augustus in AD 6.

name: Herod Antipas
summary: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, was tetrarch of Galilee and Perea (4 BC - AD 39). He married Herodias, his brother Philip's wife; rebuked by John the Baptist, he imprisoned him and, trapped by an oath at his birthday feast, had him beheaded. Jesus called him 'that fox'; at the Passion Pilate sent Jesus to him, and he mocked him and sent him back.
catholic: Antipas is a figure of conscience stifled by pride and human respect: he 'heard John gladly' yet killed him rather than break a rash oath before his guests. The early Church remembered him with Pilate among those gathered against God's 'holy servant Jesus' (Acts 4:27). Rome later exiled him (Josephus).
know: Tetrarch of Galilee (Lk 3:1) - the 'Herod' of Jesus' ministry.
Beheaded John the Baptist (Mk 6:14-29).
Called 'that fox' by Jesus (Lk 13:32).
Mocked Jesus and became friends with Pilate (Lk 23:8-12).

relations.type: took the wife of his brother

name: Philip the tetrarch
summary: Philip, son of Herod the Great and brother of Antipas, was tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (4 BC - AD 34) in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Lk 3:1). He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi, where Peter would confess Jesus as the Christ.
know: Named in Luke 3:1.
Founder of Caesarea Philippi (Mt 16:13) - historically known from Josephus.
Married Salome, daughter of Herodias (Josephus).
Most scholars distinguish him from Herodias's first husband.

name: Philip, first husband of Herodias
summary: The Gospels call Herodias 'his brother Philip's wife' (Mt 14:3; Mk 6:17): this Philip, a son of Herod the Great, was her first husband before she left him for Herod Antipas.
know: Josephus calls Herodias's first husband Herod (often called Herod II or 'Herod Philip'), a son of Herod the Great who held no territory.
Most scholars distinguish him from Philip the tetrarch of Luke 3:1.
Father of Salome according to Josephus.

name: Herodias
summary: Herodias, granddaughter of Herod the Great, left her husband Philip to marry his brother Herod Antipas. When John the Baptist declared the marriage unlawful, she nursed a grudge against him, and at Herod's birthday feast she prompted her daughter to ask for John's head on a platter.
catholic: Herodias is often compared with Jezebel, who persecuted Elijah, since Jesus identifies John with Elijah. John's death for rebuking her marriage makes him a martyr for the indissolubility and holiness of marriage.
know: Wife first of Philip, then of his brother Herod Antipas (Mk 6:17).
Held a grudge against John the Baptist (Mk 6:19).
Prompted her daughter to request John's head (Mt 14:8).

name: Salome, daughter of Herodias
summary: The 'daughter of Herodias' danced at Herod Antipas's birthday feast and so pleased him that he swore to give her whatever she asked; prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter.
know: The Gospels do not name her; the name Salome comes from the historian Josephus.
Josephus says she later married Philip the tetrarch.
Distinct from Salome the disciple at the cross (Mk 15:40).

name: Pontius Pilate
summary: Pontius Pilate was Roman prefect of Judea (AD 26-36). At the Passion he questioned Jesus about his kingship ('What is truth?'), found no basis for a charge, sent him to Herod, offered to release him, then had him scourged, presented him to the crowd, released Barabbas, washed his hands, and handed Jesus over to be crucified, posting the inscription 'King of the Jews'.
catholic: Pilate is named in the Creed - 'suffered under Pontius Pilate' - which anchors the Passion in real, datable history. The Church sees in him the weakness of a judge who knew the truth but yielded to fear and expediency. His existence is confirmed by Roman historians and by the 'Pilate stone' found at Caesarea in 1961.
know: Prefect of Judea, AD 26-36 (Lk 3:1).
'What is truth?' (Jn 18:38).
Washed his hands before the crowd (Mt 27:24).
Named in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds.

name: Caiaphas
summary: Joseph Caiaphas, son-in-law of Annas, was high priest (c. AD 18-36). He counselled the Sanhedrin that it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish, presided over Jesus' night trial, tore his robes at Jesus' claim to be the Christ, and sent him to Pilate. He later interrogated Peter and John.
catholic: John notes that Caiaphas unwittingly prophesied that Jesus would die 'for the nation, and not for the nation only, but ... to gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad' (Jn 11:51-52; CCC 596). An ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', found in Jerusalem in 1990, is widely thought to be his family's.
know: High priest 'that year' (Jn 11:49).
Son-in-law of Annas (Jn 18:13).
Presided at Jesus' trial before the council (Mt 26:57-66).
Questioned Peter and John (Acts 4:6).

name: Annas
summary: Annas had been high priest (AD 6-15) and remained the senior power in the priestly family; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him. After his arrest Jesus was led first to Annas, who questioned him about his disciples and teaching before sending him bound to Caiaphas.
catholic: Luke's phrase 'the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas' (Lk 3:2) reflects Annas's continuing authority. With Caiaphas he later confronted the apostles in Acts 4.
know: Father-in-law of Caiaphas (Jn 18:13).
Questioned Jesus first after his arrest (Jn 18:19-24).
Named with Caiaphas in Luke 3:2 and Acts 4:6.

name: Tiberius Caesar
summary: Tiberius succeeded Augustus as emperor (AD 14-37). Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to 'the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar' (Lk 3:1), and Jesus' public life, death and resurrection took place under his rule.
catholic: The 'Caesar' whose image was on the denarius when Jesus said 'Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mt 22:21) was Tiberius - a key text for Catholic teaching on the relation of Church and state. Antipas named the city of Tiberias, on the Sea of Tiberias, after him (Jn 6:1).
know: Emperor AD 14-37; adopted son and successor of Augustus.
His fifteenth year dates John's ministry (Lk 3:1).
Reigning emperor during Jesus' ministry and crucifixion.

name: Caesar Augustus
summary: Augustus, the first Roman emperor (27 BC - AD 14), issued the decree that 'all the world should be enrolled', which brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, the city of David, where Jesus was born.
catholic: Luke sets the birth of the Prince of Peace in the reign of the emperor hailed as bringer of the Pax Romana and 'saviour', quietly contrasting the two. The Fathers saw God's providence using the census to fulfil the prophecy that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem (Mic 5:2).
know: First Roman emperor.
His census decree brought the Holy Family to Bethlehem (Lk 2:1-4).
Reigned when Jesus was born.

name: Quirinius
summary: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was governor of Syria; Luke dates the enrollment that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem as 'the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria' (Lk 2:2).
know: Named in Luke 2:2.
The dating is debated, since Josephus records a census under Quirinius in AD 6; proposed solutions include an earlier administrative role or reading 'first' as 'before'.

name: Lysanias
summary: Lysanias is named as tetrarch of Abilene in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, when the word of God came to John the Baptist (Lk 3:1).
know: Named only in Luke 3:1.
An inscription from Abila confirms a tetrarch Lysanias in the early first century AD.
